question: Does indexed polynomial evaluation reduce memory and execution time across every measured MIS case?
conclusion: Indexed evaluation consistently reduces additional peak memory, while execution time improves in only part of the strong-MIS cases and is slower in every weak-MIS case by the measured median.

panels.a: Boundary evidence: all 12 dense/indexed forward-backward time ratios, with observed timing-range envelopes, prevent a blanket speedup claim.
panels.b: Primary resource evidence: additional peak allocated-memory ratios establish the consistent memory reduction across all 12 cases.

data_policy: All 12 requested configurations are retained; no observation or timing block is excluded. Raw values are copied to source-data.json.

statistics.time_center: Median dense block mean divided by median indexed block mean; five blocks of five iterations per kernel.
statistics.time_interval: Descriptive envelope from minimum dense block mean / maximum indexed block mean to maximum dense block mean / minimum indexed block mean; not a confidence interval or paired-block interval.
statistics.memory_center: Peak additional allocated bytes above the resident baseline, dense divided by indexed.
statistics.memory_interval: Not applicable: one peak measurement per kernel over the measured iterations.
statistics.replicate_unit: One fixed generated graph per n,k pair; weak and strong definitions share that graph. Timing blocks are technical repetitions, not independent graph samples.

limitations: Microkernel forward/backward only, not end-to-end neural training or solver timing.
Sequential dense-then-indexed measurements without temperature or power controls.
Float32 reduction roundoff differs; no claim of identical training trajectories.
Both representations remain resident; memory ratios use additional peak above that shared baseline.
